title: Programming glossary
description: Understand common programming terms through clear explanations and examples. Start with static websites, then meet Git, Node.js, Next.js, and the services that ship them.
noResults: No matching terms. Try another word.

demo.pageMessage: This page comes from a prepared HTML file.
demo.note: Click the page button: only the browser count changes. Visit again to receive the same HTML and restart the browser count at zero.
demo.noJs: The definition and diagram work without JavaScript. Enable JavaScript to try the buttons.
demo.caveat: This is a simplified local demonstration. It sends no network requests. Real visits can reuse browser or CDN caches.

static-website.title: Static website
static-website.description: A website whose HTML is prepared before a visit and delivered as page files.

meaning.heading: What static means
meaning.definition: A static website serves prepared HTML pages and related files, including styles, images, and JavaScript. The server does not need to assemble new HTML for that visit.
meaning.analogy: Consider a personal introduction. You put your name, experience, and work into page files, then publish them online. When a reader opens that address, the server delivers the page you already published.
meaning.keyPoint: The key question is when the HTML is generated, rather than whether the page has animations, buttons, or interactions.

how-it-works.heading: What happens when you open the site
how-it-works.intro: Start with a common case: the browser needs to fetch the page and has no cached response it can reuse.
how-it-works.prepare: Prepare the files. An author writes HTML or a build tool generates it in advance, before a reader visits.
how-it-works.deploy: Publish the files. Put HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images on a server that can deliver them.
how-it-works.request: Request the page. A reader opens a URL. The browser requests its HTML, and the server returns the prepared file.
how-it-works.render: Display the page. The browser reads the HTML, loads the styles, images, and scripts it needs, then displays the result and runs interactions.
how-it-works.cache: A real visit does not always download every file again. Browser caches and a CDN can reuse content. A CDN is a service with servers in different places that can deliver content nearby; using one does not determine whether a website is static.

example.heading: A small website example
example.intro: A simple portfolio can consist of these files. You do not need to memorize the code; first understand each file’s job.
example.html: index.html contains the structure and initial content, such as a title, introduction, and button.
example.css: style.css controls fonts, colors, spacing, and layouts for different screens.
example.js: script.js runs in the browser, for example to count button clicks.
example.codeIntro: The HTML can prepare a heading and counter button, then load a script:
example.scriptIntro: The script can update the number on the button inside the browser:
example.change: Clicking the button updates the current page in the browser. It does not rewrite the server’s HTML file, so the website can still be served statically.
example.generated: Static pages do not all need to be written by hand. A static site generator can turn articles and templates into HTML in advance, then publish the generated files.

interaction.heading: Try an interactive static page
interaction.intro: Click the page button and compare the browser count with the HTML response count. Then choose “Visit again” and see which number changes.
interaction.explanation: The first click changes a number in browser memory. “Visit again” simulates receiving the initial HTML again, so this example starts the count at zero. A real site can also save state in the browser and restore it on a later visit.

comparison.heading: Static and dynamic websites
comparison.intro: This comparison concerns how the server supplies HTML. Whether a page can change in the browser is a separate question.

work.label: Server work
work.static: Find and return an existing file
work.dynamic: Run application logic and produce a response

data.label: Data in the HTML
data.static: Usually added during authoring or a build
data.dynamic: Can be read from a database or another source for the request

updates.label: Updating published text
updates.static: Edit files, or rebuild and publish
updates.dynamic: Generate a page from updated data

comparison.mixed: One product can use both approaches: prepare public introduction pages in advance and generate account pages for each request. A static page can also call an API after loading to show current data. A button or screenshot alone cannot tell you how the initial HTML was supplied.

uses.heading: When a static website fits
uses.intro: Consider a static website when the main task is publishing content and most readers can receive the same initial page.
uses.portfolio: Personal sites and portfolios: introduce yourself, show projects, and share contact details.
uses.publishing: Blogs, tutorials, and product documentation: authors publish content that readers browse as pages.
uses.marketing: Product and event pages: display public information, with browser scripts for animation or a calculator.
uses.benefits: Prepared files are often straightforward to cache and distribute. They can also reduce the server logic needed to generate pages. Actual speed and cost still depend on images, scripts, traffic, and hosting.
uses.limits: Login, shared comments, payments, live inventory, and stored submissions require the appropriate services and interfaces. The frontend can still be served statically, but public HTML files alone do not implement those functions.

frozen.title: Does static mean the content never changes?
frozen.body: No. Authors can edit and republish files. Static describes how HTML is supplied for a visit, rather than how often the site is updated.

server.title: Does a static website have no server?
server.body: An online visit still needs a server or CDN to deliver files. You may not need to maintain an application that generates HTML, but the files still need hosting and delivery.

database.title: Can a static site use a database?
database.body: A build can read a database or content management system. The browser can also fetch data through an API. Supplying the initial HTML and fetching later data are separate steps.

security.title: Can frontend files store a secret API key?
security.body: Do not put secret keys in public HTML or JavaScript. Readers can inspect files delivered to their browser. Operations that need secrets should use an appropriate server-side interface.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: A portfolio generates all its HTML in advance. It has animations, filter buttons, and a weather API call. Can it still be a static website?
recap.reason: Its initial HTML exists before the visit. Animations, filtering, and later API requests run in the browser; they do not turn the initial HTML into a response generated for that request.
recap.remember: Ask this question: When someone opens the page, does the server return existing HTML or generate HTML for that request?

references.intro: These official guides explain static content, file hosting, browser interactions, and caching.

references.server: MDN: what a web server does

git.title: Git
git.description: A version control tool that records every change to your code, so you can return to earlier versions and work on the same project with others.

meaning.heading: What is Git?
meaning.definition: Git is a version control tool. It saves the project's files as a snapshot at each stage, along with who changed what and when. Think of it as a photo album you can flip backward: every photo is a version.
meaning.analogy: It works like save points in a game: save at each level, and if things go wrong later, load an earlier save. Git stores code and files rather than game progress.
meaning.keyPoint: Git manages the version history. GitHub is just a website that hosts Git repositories.

how-it-works.heading: What does one commit do?
how-it-works.intro: Start with the four steps you will use most. These commands run on your own computer and need no network.

steps.init: Run git init in the project folder. Git creates a repository and starts tracking changes there.
steps.stage: Use git add to choose the changes for this snapshot. Anything you leave out waits for next time.
steps.commit: Run git commit. Git stores the chosen changes as a snapshot with a message, an author, and a time.
steps.branch: Later you can return to an old version, or create a branch, work on a separate line, and merge it back.

how-it-works.note: Commits happen locally. You only need the network for git push or when fetching from a remote.

example.heading: A real commit, step by step
example.intro: Suppose you have just written a homepage and want to record it in the version history.

points.repo: git init: turns the current folder into a Git repository and adds a hidden .git directory.
points.snapshot: git add and git commit: choose the changes, then store them as a snapshot with a message.
points.history: git log: lists every commit, each with its own ID called a commit hash.

example.codeIntro: Three commands: create the repository, choose the changes, and store the snapshot.
example.afterCode: The first version of index.html is now saved. Every later change and commit adds another page to the history.

comparison.heading: How is Git different from copying a folder?
comparison.intro: Manual backups also keep old versions, but the method is very different.

stores.label: What is kept
stores.left: The full history of every commit

restore.label: Finding an old version
restore.left: Check out any commit at any time
restore.right: Search backup folders and hope you pick the right one

team.label: Working with others
team.left: Each person uses a branch, then merges
team.right: Changes overwrite each other, and nobody knows who changed what

comparison.mixed: Git also works with cloud storage or GitHub: commit locally as usual, then sync the repository so others can see and pull it.

uses.heading: When should you use Git?
uses.intro: Any project that keeps changing is worth tracking, especially when several people work on it.

items.personal: Personal projects: undo a bad change and try new ideas on a branch.
items.team: Team work: everyone changes their own branch, then merges into the main one.
items.open-source: Open source: fork a repository, make changes, then open a merge request.

uses.benefits: Branches are cheap in Git, so creating one takes almost no time. The full history makes every change traceable.
uses.limits: Git is not good at storing large binary files, and it is not automatic backup. If the repository is lost and was never synced, its history is lost too.

github.title: Are Git and GitHub the same thing?
github.body: No. Git is a tool on your computer; GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories. You can also use GitLab, Gitea, or just Git on your own machine.

upload.title: Does commit mean upload?
upload.body: No. A commit saves changes to the local repository. Uploading needs another step, git push, which sends local commits to a remote.

branch-weight.title: Are branches expensive?
branch-weight.body: No. A Git branch is just a label pointing at a commit, so creating one is nearly free. Make as many as you need.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: You broke the code, but you committed earlier. How do you get back to the previous commit?
recap.reason: The previous commit is still complete in the repository. You can check it out to look, or make a new commit that restores the files to that state.
recap.remember: Remember: Git stores a chain of commits, not just the latest file.

references.heading: Read further
references.intro: These references are a good next step.

links.branching: Pro Git: What a branch is

node-js.title: Node.js
node-js.description: A runtime that lets JavaScript run outside the browser, often used for web backends, command-line tools, and developer tooling.

meaning.heading: What is Node.js?
meaning.definition: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime. JavaScript used to run only in browsers; Node.js lets it run on your own computer or on a server.
meaning.analogy: A browser is one home for JavaScript; Node.js is another. The language stays the same, but the furniture is different.
meaning.keyPoint: JavaScript is the language. Node.js is the environment that runs it.

how-it-works.heading: How does a program run?
how-it-works.intro: Write some JavaScript, hand it to Node.js, and it can read files, open a server, and more.

steps.write: Write a .js or .mjs file containing the program you want to run.
steps.run: Run node filename in the terminal. Node.js reads and executes the file.
steps.capabilities: The program can read and write files, make network requests, and connect to databases, which browsers normally cannot do.
steps.serve: It can also start a server that waits for requests, such as a website backend API.

how-it-works.note: Node.js runs JavaScript and provides these capabilities. It does not dictate how you organize the project.

example.heading: A tiny Node.js server
example.intro: This program starts a server and answers each visit with a short message.

points.file: Save it as server.mjs. node:http ships with Node.js, so there is nothing to install.
points.result: Open http://localhost:3000 and you should see Hello from Node.js.

example.codeIntro: The code uses only modules that ship with Node.js.
example.afterCode: The server keeps running until you press Ctrl+C in the terminal.

comparison.heading: How is Node.js different from JavaScript in a browser?
comparison.intro: The language is the same, but each environment can do different things.

where.label: Where it runs
where.left: On your computer or a server
where.right: In the browser showing the page

can.label: What it can do
can.left: Read files, run servers, connect to databases
can.right: Update the page, respond to clicks, make network requests

cannot.label: What it cannot do
cannot.right: Freely read and write files on the user's computer

comparison.mixed: You can use one language for frontend and backend, but the code runs in different places and has different powers.

uses.heading: When is Node.js a good fit?
uses.intro: Node.js is a good fit whenever something should happen outside the browser.

items.backend: Web backends: receive requests, query a database, and return data.
items.cli: Command-line tools: batch-edit files, generate projects, and run scripts.
items.tooling: Developer tooling: many build tools and dev servers run on Node.js themselves.

uses.benefits: One language for frontend and backend lowers switching costs, and npm has a huge collection of ready-made packages.
uses.limits: It handles one thing at a time by default, so heavy computation can block other requests. You also have to deploy and maintain the server.

language.title: Is Node.js a programming language?
language.body: No. The language is JavaScript; Node.js is the environment that runs JavaScript.

browser.title: Can Node.js only run on servers?
browser.body: No. You can use it on your own computer for scripts and file work, with no network and no deployment.

framework.title: Is Node.js a framework?
framework.body: No. It does not prescribe routes, pages, or folder structure. Express and Next.js are frameworks.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: Can you call document.querySelector in Node.js to manipulate a page?
recap.reason: Node.js has no page and no browser DOM. It works with files, networks, and servers instead.
recap.remember: Remember: JavaScript is the language; Node.js lets it run outside the browser.

references.heading: Read further
references.intro: These references are a good next step.

next-js.title: Next.js
next-js.description: A full-stack web framework built on React that brings routing, rendering, data fetching, and build tooling together.

meaning.heading: What is Next.js?
meaning.definition: Next.js is a web framework built on top of React. React turns a page into components; Next.js adds routing, rendering modes, data fetching, and a production build.
meaning.analogy: If React is a box of building blocks, Next.js is the instructions, the toolbox, and the assembly line: same blocks, but a consistent way to assemble and ship them.
meaning.keyPoint: Next.js is not a new language or a replacement for React. It is a set of conventions on top of React.

how-it-works.heading: From a new project to a live site
how-it-works.intro: Next.js has an established path for the usual steps from a new project to a live site.

steps.create: Create the project with create-next-app. The folder structure, configuration, and dev server are ready at once.
steps.page: Add page files in the app directory. The file path becomes the URL.
steps.render: Choose server rendering, browser rendering, or a page generated ahead of time, depending on the page.
steps.build: Run the build command. Next.js bundles and optimizes the assets, then a hosting platform publishes them.

how-it-works.note: These conventions remove a lot of configuration, but the project has to follow the framework's rules.

example.heading: The smallest page
example.intro: A minimal Next.js page is a file that exports a React component.

points.file: The file goes at app/page.tsx and exports a default component.
points.route: app/page.tsx is the home page /; add app/about/page.tsx and you get /about.
points.result: Start the dev server and open the home page to see the heading.

example.codeIntro: The file is both the page and the route.
example.afterCode: There is no separate route table: the file's location decides the URL.

comparison.heading: How is Next.js different from React alone?
comparison.intro: React handles the interface. Next.js turns that interface into a site you can ship.

routing.label: Page routing
routing.right: Choose and configure a router yourself

rendering.label: Rendering
rendering.left: Server rendering, static generation, or client rendering

build.label: Build and deploy
build.left: Bundling, optimization, and deploy conventions included

comparison.mixed: You can build a complete site with React alone, but routing, rendering, and bundling are yours to wire up. Next.js makes those common choices up front.

uses.heading: When is Next.js a good fit?
uses.intro: Next.js fits sites that need pages and backend endpoints, or that care about first paint and search indexing.

items.content: Content sites: blogs, docs, and courses whose pages can be generated ahead of time.
items.seo: Pages that search engines must read: server rendering puts the content in the initial HTML.
items.fullstack: Full-stack apps for small teams: pages and endpoints live in one project.

uses.benefits: Clear conventions, batteries included, and static pages and dynamic endpoints can coexist.
uses.limits: The framework has its own rules and version changes. For a handful of static pages, it can feel heavy.

react-replacement.title: Does Next.js replace React?
react-replacement.body: No. Next.js uses React internally, and you still need React to write pages.

always-fast.title: Is a Next.js site always fast?
always-fast.body: No. Image size, data requests, and rendering choices all affect speed. The framework only provides the tools.

vercel-only.title: Can Next.js only deploy to Vercel?
vercel-only.body: No. Vercel is the platform from the same company and the least effort, but Next.js can also run in other Node.js environments.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: What do you usually do to add an /about page in Next.js?
recap.reason: Put a component-exporting file at app/about/page.tsx and the route exists. No separate registration is needed.
recap.remember: Remember: Next.js maps file paths to URLs and uses conventions to cut configuration.

references.heading: Read further
references.intro: These references are a good next step.

vercel.title: Vercel
vercel.description: A hosting platform for frontends and Next.js. Push code to a Git repository, and it builds and publishes the site to a global network.

meaning.heading: What is Vercel?
meaning.definition: Vercel is a hosting platform. You put the site's code in a Git repository, and Vercel builds it, publishes it, and serves pages from locations close to visitors.
meaning.analogy: It is like handing finished pages to a delivery chain: you drop them at the depot, and it copies and distributes them to local shops.
meaning.keyPoint: Vercel runs and delivers your site. It does not write the code for you.

how-it-works.heading: What happens when you push code?
how-it-works.intro: The common setup connects a Git repository so every push publishes automatically.

steps.connect: Connect a Git repository in Vercel and choose the project to deploy.
steps.push: Each push notifies Vercel, which starts a new build.
steps.build: Vercel installs dependencies and runs the build command to produce the deployable files.
steps.serve: A successful build is published, and every push also gets a preview URL.

how-it-works.note: A failed build does not replace the live version. You can read the logs and decide whether to retry.

example.heading: Publish from the command line
example.intro: You can also publish a project manually from the terminal.

points.install: Install the Vercel command-line tool first.
points.preview: Run vercel, sign in, confirm the settings, and you get a preview URL.
points.production: Run vercel --prod to publish this build to the production domain.

example.codeIntro: Three commands: install, preview, and publish to production.
example.afterCode: The first run asks a few questions, such as the project name and framework. After that, you can publish repeatedly.

comparison.heading: How is Vercel different from renting a server?
comparison.intro: Both put a site online. The difference is who manages the machines.

deploy.label: How you publish
deploy.left: Push code and the build deploys itself
deploy.right: Log in, pull the code, and restart the service

ops.label: Who maintains the machine
ops.right: You handle the OS, security, and scaling

control.label: How much control
control.left: Follow the platform's rules; less work, fewer options
control.right: Change anything, but build everything yourself

comparison.mixed: You can also use Vercel only for the frontend and keep the API and database elsewhere. The whole project does not have to live on the platform.

uses.heading: When is Vercel a good fit?
uses.intro: Vercel fits frontend-heavy projects where a push should be enough to go live.

items.nextjs: Next.js projects: platform and framework come from the same company, so setup is minimal.
items.preview: Team review: every branch or push can produce a preview URL.
items.static: Static sites and docs: build once and distribute to nodes around the world.

uses.benefits: Automatic builds, preview URLs, and global delivery remove a lot of server work.
uses.limits: Free quotas are limited and costs rise with usage. The platform has its own limits, so complex backends usually belong elsewhere.

next-only.title: Can Vercel only deploy Next.js?
next-only.body: No. It supports many frontend frameworks and static sites, though its Next.js support is the most complete.

git-host.title: Is Vercel a code host like GitHub?
git-host.body: No. The code still lives in a Git repository. Vercel reads that repository and handles the build and publish.

secrets.title: Is it safe to put keys in the code and deploy?
secrets.body: No. Keep secrets in environment variables. Do not commit them to the repository or expose them in browser code.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: What does Vercel do every time you push code to the Git repository?
recap.reason: It receives the push, installs dependencies, and runs the build. On success it publishes and creates a preview URL.
recap.remember: Remember: Vercel turns a code push into an automatic release.

references.heading: Read further
references.intro: These references are a good next step.

cloudflare.title: Cloudflare
cloudflare.description: A global network service for CDN, DNS, protection, and edge computing that makes sites faster and safer.

meaning.heading: What is Cloudflare?
meaning.definition: Cloudflare is a global network service. Once a site's domain is managed by Cloudflare, visitor requests reach a nearby Cloudflare node first, which either returns a cached copy or forwards the request to your server.
meaning.analogy: Think of the guard and parcel locker at a building entrance: visitors are checked at the door, and frequently used items are kept nearby instead of fetched from far away.
meaning.keyPoint: Cloudflare sits in front of your server and handles caching, acceleration, and filtering.

how-it-works.heading: Where does a request go?
how-it-works.intro: Take the most common case, speeding up a website. A request goes through these steps.

steps.nameserver: Point the domain's DNS servers at Cloudflare, which then handles name resolution.
steps.edge: The visitor's request reaches the Cloudflare node closest to them.
steps.cache: If that node has a usable cached copy, it answers directly; otherwise it fetches one from your origin.
steps.protect: Along the way, Cloudflare filters malicious traffic, provides HTTPS, and records request details.

how-it-works.note: The origin is the server that actually holds your site. Cloudflare does not store your code; it handles requests that pass through it.

example.heading: Read the cache from a response header
example.intro: A response header shows whether Cloudflare handled the request.

points.dns: First confirm the domain is on Cloudflare and the proxy is enabled.
points.headers: Use curl to inspect the response headers and find server and cf-cache-status.
points.cache: cf-cache-status of HIT means the cached copy was used; MISS means the origin was asked for fresh content.

example.codeIntro: This command only sends one request. It changes nothing.
example.afterCode: Headers vary between sites, but server: cloudflare usually means the request passed through Cloudflare.

comparison.heading: How is it different from connecting directly to a server?
comparison.intro: Adding a network layer changes the path a request takes.

distance.label: Distance to the visitor
distance.right: Connects to wherever the origin is

protection.label: Protection
protection.left: Can block attacks and hide the origin address
protection.right: The origin is exposed and must protect itself

cache.label: Caching
cache.left: Static assets can live on nodes worldwide
cache.right: Every request goes to the origin

comparison.mixed: Dynamic content should not be cached for long. You can cache only images, styles, and scripts while pages still come from the origin.

uses.heading: When is Cloudflare a good fit?
uses.intro: Add Cloudflare when a site needs to be faster, more resilient, or safer.

items.cdn: Static asset delivery: images, styles, and scripts cached on nodes worldwide.
items.dns: DNS and HTTPS: manage records in one place and issue certificates automatically.
items.protection: Protection: block malicious traffic and common web attacks.

uses.benefits: Many global nodes, a usable free plan, and onboarding that often only needs a DNS change.
uses.limits: Cache rules must match the content, and a wrong rule shows visitors an old page. Dynamic requests gain little if the origin itself is slow.

hosting.title: Is Cloudflare web hosting?
hosting.body: Not exactly. It mainly handles DNS, caching, protection, and edge logic. The site's files usually stay on your own server or another hosting platform.

always-fast.title: Is a site always faster with Cloudflare?
always-fast.body: No. Static assets speed up when the cache hits. If the origin is slow or caching is not configured, the gain can be small.

replace-server.title: Does Cloudflare mean you can drop your server?
replace-server.body: Usually not. It forwards requests to you, and the origin still generates the pages. Products such as Workers can run code at the edge, but that is a separate job.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: A visitor requests an image, and the Cloudflare node has it cached. What happens?
recap.reason: The request never reaches the origin, so the visitor gets the image sooner and the origin does less work.
recap.remember: Remember: Cloudflare stands in front of the origin: cache and check first, then decide whether to go back.

references.heading: Read further
references.intro: These references are a good next step.

supabase.title: Supabase
supabase.description: An open-source backend platform built on PostgreSQL that provides a database, authentication, file storage, and realtime subscriptions.

meaning.heading: What is Supabase?
meaning.definition: Supabase is a backend platform. It packages a database, authentication, file storage, and realtime updates so a frontend can call them directly instead of building a backend from scratch.
meaning.analogy: It is like a fitted kitchen: the stove, fridge, and plumbing are already connected, so you can start cooking with your ingredients.
meaning.keyPoint: PostgreSQL is at the core of Supabase. The other features are built around it.

how-it-works.heading: From an empty project to live data
how-it-works.intro: Getting from an empty project to a frontend that reads and writes data usually takes these steps.

steps.project: Create a Supabase project and get its URL and a publishable API key.
steps.schema: Create tables in the database and define what each column stores.
steps.query: The frontend queries or writes through the official SDK, which calls generated APIs.
steps.auth: Turn on authentication and set row-level security (RLS) to decide who may read and write.

how-it-works.note: Row-level security is a database rule, not a hidden frontend button. Hiding a button still leaves the API callable.

example.heading: Query the notes table
example.intro: This code reads every row from the notes table.

points.client: Create a client with the project URL and the publishable key.
points.query: from('notes').select('*') asks for every column in the notes table.
points.result: data holds the rows and error holds any failure. Handle both.

example.codeIntro: This query also runs in the browser.
example.afterCode: With RLS enabled, the signed-in user and the rules decide which rows come back. The key can be public, but the rules cannot be skipped.

comparison.heading: How is Supabase different from building a backend?
comparison.intro: Both can serve data. The difference is who builds the infrastructure.

database.label: Database
database.right: Install, back up, and maintain it yourself

auth.label: Authentication
auth.left: Accounts, social sign-in, and permissions built in
auth.right: Build it or connect another service

ops.label: Operations
ops.left: The platform handles upgrades and availability
ops.right: You watch the server and scale it

comparison.mixed: Supabase can also be self-hosted. When the business logic gets complex, you can still write your own server code and connect it to the same database.

uses.heading: When is Supabase a good fit?
uses.intro: Supabase fits apps that need sign-in and stored data without a from-scratch backend.

items.prototype: Prototypes and MVPs: get the main flow working before building a full backend.
items.team: Small teams: database, authentication, and file storage in one setup.
items.realtime: Realtime collaboration: changes can be pushed to the page someone is viewing.

uses.benefits: Ready to use, built on standard PostgreSQL, and your data can be exported at any time.
uses.limits: The platform hides some details, while complex permissions and business logic are still your design. Free projects also have limited resources.

just-database.title: Is Supabase just a database?
just-database.body: No. The database is the core, but authentication, storage, realtime, and APIs come with it.

anon-key.title: Is it safe to put the publishable API key in a web page?
anon-key.body: The key itself can be public, but it must be paired with RLS. Without rules, people may read data they should not see.

small-only.title: Is Supabase only for small projects?
small-only.body: No. You can pay for more capacity or self-host, but at larger scale you still need to understand databases and permissions.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: If the frontend queries Supabase directly, how do you stop one user from seeing another user's data?
recap.reason: Rules in the database are tied to the signed-in user, so a query returns only allowed rows instead of relying on hidden frontend controls.
recap.remember: Remember: Supabase packages the backend, but you still define the permission rules.
